alignment.note: The Greek aorist participle ἀναστενάξας ('having sighed deeply') is rendered by the Vulgate present participle ingemiscens and by the Syriac finite verb ܘܐܬܬܢܚ ('and he groaned'), an Ethpaʿʿal form coordinated with the following verb; Syriac thus prefers paratactic coordination where Greek subordinates by participle.
πνεύματι / ܒܪܘܚܗ / spiritu — the Vulgate omits the article-bearing dative construction but the sense is identical.
The Greek possessive αὐτοῦ ('his') is expressed in Syriac by the pronominal suffix on ܒܪܘܚܗ ('in his spirit') and is left implicit in the Latin spiritu, which carries no possessive marker.

Greek λέγει (historic present) and Syriac ܘܐܡܪ (coordinated finite verb) introduce direct speech; the Vulgate ait followed by colon punctuation marks the same transition, the colon (idx 4) functioning as the discourse boundary.
τί / ܡܢܐ / Quid — interrogative opening the rhetorical question.
ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη / ܫܪܒܬܐ ܗܕܐ / generatio ista ('this generation'); Greek supplies the article, which Syriac and Latin lack but render with the demonstrative.

All three attest the verb 'seeks' (ζητεῖ / ܒܥܝܐ / quærit), but the word order differs: Greek and Latin place the verb after the object 'sign' (Latin signum quærit), whereas Syriac fronts the verb ܒܥܝܐ before its object ܐܬܐ.
σημεῖον; / ܐܬܐ / signum — the interrogative is marked in Greek by the question particle, in Latin by the closing '?' (idx 10), and in Syriac by context.
ἀμήν / ܐܡܝܢ / Amen — the Hebraic affirmation transliterated uniformly across all three.
λέγω / ܐܡܪ ܐܢܐ / dico — Syriac uses the periphrastic participle + enclitic pronoun ܐܢܐ to express the first-person, where Greek and Latin use a synthetic finite form.
ὑμῖν / ܠܟܘܢ / vobis — second-person plural indirect object.

Greek εἰ functions here as a Hebraism marking an emphatic oath-negation ('[surely] no sign shall be given'); the Vulgate woodenly calques this with conditional si, whereas the Syriac ܕܠܐ supplies the explicit negative ('that not'), making the suppressed apodosis of the Semitic oath formula overt.
δοθήσεται / ܬܬܝܗܒ / dabitur — future/imperfect passive 'shall be given'.

The Peshitta adds the resumptive dative pronoun ܠܗ ('to it'), anticipating the following ܠܫܪܒܬܐ ܗܕܐ; this proleptic pronoun is a characteristic Syriac construction with no counterpart in the Greek or Latin.
τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ / ܠܫܪܒܬܐ ܗܕܐ / generationi isti ('to this generation'); dative/prepositional indirect object with demonstrative.
σημεῖον / ܐܬܐ / signum — the subject of the passive verb, 'a sign'.
